Exploratory research tool

This website supports literature exploration, physical circuit simulations and hypothesis generation.

  • Illustrative defaults. Simulator parameters have not been calibrated against matched cancer-cell experimental data.
  • Unvalidated cancer-outcome hypotheses. The tool does not provide validated predictions of cancer growth, death or treatment response.
  • Unscreened, non-exhaustive literature collection. Repository records are search results awaiting relevance screening. The collection is not an exhaustive systematic review.
  • Documented methods. Sources, equations, units, assumptions and the model version are available below.

Circuit model passive-tpmet-circuit-1.0 · Research-status documentation revision 1 · 2 November 2026. Numerical checks establish implementation consistency, not biological validation.

New here? Start with this guide

Use the repository to find papers and plan research. It contains 32,163 retrieved records across cancer types for 2 November 2006–2 November 2026. These are search candidates awaiting relevance screening. The site does not provide a validated prediction of treatment response.

1. Find papers
  1. Wait for the repository count to load. Search a title phrase, author, DOI or PMID. The search uses a simple text match, not Boolean operators.
  2. Choose a topic, publication type and first-publication year range. Choose “All topics” to search across the collection. Try “breast”, “leukemia”, “glioblastoma” or an author surname.
  3. Use Previous and Next to move through 25 records per page. Click a paper title to open its Europe PMC record and follow available journal or full-text links.

Topic tags indicate which search retrieved the record. They do not confirm relevance or mechanism. “Journal records” includes reviews. Preprints are labelled and have not necessarily undergone peer review.

2. Check the evidence before using a result
  1. Read the primary paper. Check the cancer model, intervention, exposure, comparator and measured endpoint.
  2. Keep plasma-membrane voltage, mitochondrial potential, fluorescence, cell counts and metabolic assays distinct.
  3. Check whether voltage and outcome were measured in the same cells and conditions. Confirm biological replicates and whether errors are SD, SEM or confidence intervals.
  4. Use the search log to inspect the exact queries and download counts. A complete download of a query does not mean every relevant paper was found.

The selected glioma evidence below is a small extracted subset. The larger repository stores bibliographic metadata, not verified effect sizes or full texts.

3. Export papers

“Export filtered CSV” downloads the currently matching records across all result pages. “Export filtered RIS” produces a reference-manager file. Check author and publication details after importing RIS. Clear filters to export the full collection. The search log and retrieval script are available beside the export buttons.

4. Import your experimental measurements
  1. Go to Your experiments and download the CSV template.
  2. Enter one measured endpoint per row. Retain study, cell line, experiment and biological-replicate identifiers.
  3. Use mV for calibrated absolute voltage, delta_mV for a calibrated voltage change, or deltaF_F for relative fluorescence. Enter numbers only in numeric columns. Do not convert fluorescence to mV without calibration.
  4. Label each row training or test. Keep an entire independent experiment in one split.
  5. Import the CSV, correct reported errors, then inspect the readiness summary. Files must be smaller than 5 MB.

Checks cover required fields, accepted units, numeric values and experiment overlap. They do not establish scientific validity or detect every data-quality problem. Imported measurements stay in this browser session and are not uploaded.

5. Understand model comparison

This section reports structural readiness of imported data. It does not fit models, calculate uncertainty or predict cell fate yet. A future analysis must choose an endpoint, account for biological replication, compare candidate models and validate on independent experiments or cell lines.

6. Record and export a prediction
  1. Write the cells, intervention, comparator, endpoint and expected direction.
  2. Specify an outcome that would contradict the prediction before collecting results.
  3. Press Record prediction. The record receives a timestamp from your browser.
  4. When results are available, record a follow-up referencing the original prediction and experiment identifiers.
  5. Press Export session before leaving. The JSON includes the selected evidence dataset, imported measurements and prediction records. Export the literature catalogue separately using CSV or RIS.

Refreshing or closing the page clears imported data and prediction records. Downloaded JSON is an archive; restoring a session from JSON is not implemented. Timestamps are a planning aid, not an immutable preregistration.

Access and troubleshooting

If you see “Log in to access”, use Continue with ChatGPT and an account authorised to view this private site. A link alone does not grant access. If the catalogue fails to load, refresh and allow it to finish downloading. If a search returns nothing, clear the topic and year filters and try a shorter phrase. Browser downloads may appear in your device’s Downloads or Files folder.

The bars reproduce published treatment-to-control ratios. They do not predict the response of a new tumour or convert voltage change into a universal growth rate.

Voltage measurements from a separate experiment

In D54 glioma cells, acute shifts from pH 7.4 to pH 6.0 depolarised the membrane by +13.5 ± 0.92 mV; shifts to pH 8.8 hyperpolarised it by −28.8 ± 6.8 mV (reported current-clamp values). The cell-count comparisons above used different pH conditions and longer exposure. These voltage and growth measurements must not be combined into an invented mV-to-growth slope.

Honasoge et al., 2014 ↗

What remains unquantified

Neuronal or synaptic depolarisationHigher glioma Ki67 in vivo

A different experiment found increased proliferation after optogenetic stimulation of glioma xenografts. The text does not supply an effect size suitable for this calculator, so no numerical prediction is shown. Venkatesh et al., 2019 ↗

AC field plus bio-nanoantennaeReduced metabolic activity

The published GBM experiment reported an approximately 50% metabolic-activity reduction after 12 hours under its tested conditions and observed caspase activation. Metabolic activity cannot be equated to a 50% loss of cells, and the experiment does not establish a resting-membrane-voltage dose response. Rawson and colleagues, 2023 ↗

Mathematics and limits

For a reported experiment, the displayed response is the within-study ratio:

Relative response (%) = 100 × (treated endpoint / matched control endpoint)
Log effect = ln(relative response / 100)

For example, the D54 pH 6.7 condition had 66% fewer cells than pH 7.2 after 3 days, so its relative response is 34% and its log ratio is ln(0.34) ≈ −1.079. This calculation describes that specific comparison only.

For the optogenetic viability measurements, ± values are transcribed as reported, without converting them to confidence intervals. No interpolation between pH levels, across time, or across cell lines is performed. Neither MTT viability nor PrestoBlue metabolism is an absolute live-cell count.

Research interpretation only. The earlier 48-hour simulator used assumed coefficients; this evidence version removes its unsupported cell-count projections. Fit a mechanistic prediction model only after collecting matched voltage, cell-cycle, apoptosis and cell-count time courses from the target cell lines.

Traceable evidence

Six extracted comparisons from two primary studies. This is a curated starting set, not a systematic review. Each row retains its own endpoint and matched control.
